source.title: Read More, Reason Deeper: Latent Workspaces for Long-Sequence Recommendation
source.authors: Renzhi Wu; Li Sheng; Zi-Kun Cui; Jun-Jie Yang; Tai Guo; Ke-Ke Zhai; Yan-Ting Li; Jerry Fu; N. Mathur; Sri Reddy; Hong Li

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-curve analysis to long-sequence recommendation models, using normalized entropy and history, reasoning-depth, and compute sweeps rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps and fitted compute-frontier exponents. Its cited language-model scaling studies are not results from this study. Overall comparisons on the ranking surfaces are not included unless they bear on a scaling version.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper for a recommendation model. It borrows the power-law form NE = Em + Am C^−αm 'following neural scaling studies' and uses the fitted exponents to rank its own model (LWR) against three other architectures. It does not test whether the power-law form holds: it reports no goodness-of-fit, no fit uncertainty, no deviation analysis and no prediction of held-out runs. The scaling axes are user-history length and depth, with training data fixed at three days, not parameters or tokens. Each family also gets its own fitted floor. The evidence and reasoning rows are LWR-versus-baseline comparisons, not results on whether a scaling law holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that LWR decouples evidence scaling from reasoning scaling. They report that it leads all evaluated families from 12K to 65K history, keeps improving with depth, has the steepest fitted frontier across 468 configurations, and beats the baselines on two surfaces. They frame this as an architecture result, not as a test of scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: This is a recommendation-model study, not a language-model pretraining sweep. It uses normalized entropy and varies history length and reasoning depth, fitting compute-efficient history–depth frontiers rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different fitted frontier exponents for the four architecture families and reports that LWR's relative position changes across history lengths.

fits_no_version.finding: For four recommendation architectures, a power law with a per-family floor is fitted to reducible NE against training compute along the compute-efficient frontier of history–depth configurations. The exponents range from 0.424 to 0.845. No fit diagnostics are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recommendation-model normalized entropy on a history/depth compute frontier follows a power law in training compute, with architecture-dependent exponents.

record.problems: The study uses internal recommendation data and an internal training platform. It reports no uncertainty or goodness-of-fit for the frontier exponents, and the text does not provide numerical curve points or fit diagnostics for the evidence and reasoning sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: The overall surface comparison in Table 1 and the compute-efficiency figures reported alongside some NE improvements were left out because they do not directly measure a scaling-law version. The 8× depth comparison with Internal Baseline 2 was also omitted because it reports a point comparison, not a fitted scaling result.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation to larger runs is checked.
All: depth is varied as a compute axis, not at a fixed parameter count.
Whether the power-law form actually holds for recommendation models. The form is assumed and fitted without any assessment of fit quality.
Fitting choices and schedules are not varied. Exponent differences across architectures are used for ranking, not examined as fit dependence.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with V5 and V7 supports overstates the study. The power-law fit is an assessment tool for the authors' own architecture, and no evidence is given on whether the form fits well. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version, since a domain-extension claim for recommenders is not among the versions, and V5 as worded lists image, video, repeated data and fine-tuning.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from fits on smaller runs.
The compute-optimal split between language-model parameter count and training tokens.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count in language models.

The study tests scaling in recommendation models, not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer; it does not establish that the same power-law form holds in those settings.
Downstream performance predictability from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not vary parameter-count conventions, training schedule, data, or fitting method, and does not report whether curves bend away from a single power law.
